      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfree/2026/oct/16/the-guardian-view-on-the-banks-too-big-to-fail-cannot-mean-too-big-to-tax</link>
      <description><p>Financiers owe their windfalls and bonuses to higher interest rates. Britain should reclaim more for the public and resist City lobbying</p><p>John Healey is planning to tax British banks, the Guardian <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026/oct/15/john-healey-raise-taxes-banks-budget">revealed</a>, in the forthcoming budget. It’s <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfree/2025/oct/26/the-guardian-view-on-the-budget-what-a-labour-chancellor-should-really-say">about time</a> for the chancellor to act. Banks have been raking it in. The campaign group <a href="https://positivemoney.org/uk/update/new-chancellor-higher-profits-its-time-to-taxthebanks/">Positive Money</a> reported&nbsp;this summer that Britain’s four biggest banks&nbsp;made £29bn in the first half of this year, up a fifth on 2025. These windfalls owe more to higher interest rates than better products or services. Households and businesses pay more to borrow. Meanwhile, the Bank of England pays the banks tens of&nbsp;billions in interest on their reserves, with the&nbsp;<a href="https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfree/2026/sep/15/the-guardian-view-on-the-bank-of-englands-120bn-bill-power-without-accountability">Treasury</a> footing the bill.</p><p>The chancellor is said to favour restoring the bank surcharge from 3% to 8%, which could raise around <a href="https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c32l4k2xdvrzo">£2bn a year</a>.&nbsp;This would recover a very modest share of the&nbsp;sector’s bonanza. Louis XIV’s finance minister, Jean-Baptiste Colbert, said that “the art of taxation consists in so plucking the goose as to obtain the largest possible amount of feathers with the smallest possible amount of hissing”. Britain’s banks have plenty of feathers. That hasn’t stopped them <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/aug/17/jp-morgan-boss-jamie-dimon-warns-uk-chancellor-windfall-tax-banks">hissing</a>. The banks say that they already face <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/sep/02/british-banks-pressure-burnham-tax-profits-john-healey">higher</a> taxes than other companies, that they won’t be able to lend as much, and that their profits won’t last.</p><p><em><strong>Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article?       <title>Move over, pervert glasses – the latest toxic trend is robogroping</title>
      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfree/2026/oct/17/smartglasses-robogroping-toxic-trends</link>
      <description><p>Whenever a new technology is created, it will, without exception, immediately be used to harass girls and women</p><p>You may be familiar with <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rule_34">rule 34</a> of the internet, which states that if something exists or can be imagined, there will almost certainly be online porn of it. Now let me introduce my rule 35: whenever a new technology is created, it will, without exception, immediately be used to harass girls and women.</p><p>See, for example, Meta’s “<a href="https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfree/2026/aug/31/law-meta-pervert-glasses-mockery">pervert glasses</a>”. As anyone could have foreseen, putting a tiny camera and microphone into smartglasses would immediately lead to people using them to record and harass women. Lo and behold, that is exactly what happened. So-called manfluencers have <a href="https://www.cnn.com/2026/02/09/world/manfluencers-smart-glasses-intl">filmed themselves</a> trying to flirt with women in public spaces and then uploaded the footage to TikTok. The women in these videos are often not aware they’ve been recorded until their identities are shared online and they are <a href="https://www.404media.co/meta-ray-ban-smart-glasses-pov-instagram-pickup-artists/">harassed</a> by strangers. And what’s Meta doing about this? It’s instituted a few bans and made some privacy updates, but doesn’t seem to have an appetite to properly solve the problem. Indeed, at the Meta Connect 2026 keynote, Mark Zuckerberg did <a href="https://www.tomsguide.com/computing/smart-glasses/what-was-missing-from-meta-connect-2026-an-apology">not feel the need</a> to apologize to the women whose lives have been upended by his technology.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfree/2026/oct/17/smartglasses-robogroping-toxic-trends">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <title>The hill I will die on: Cinemas have been getting away with lies. Films should begin on time | Jeffrey Ingold</title>

      <description><p>If cinemas must run 20 minutes of adverts before a feature, they could at least be honest about it. Or, I have a better solution …</p><p>Do you remember the last time you were lied to? I certainly do. I was tricked by the North Finchley Vue, which sold me and my boyfriend tickets to a 7.15pm showing of The Odyssey. Guess what was playing at 7.15pm? A car advert. Ten minutes later, it was a trailer for the horror film Werwulf. Then there was an advert for Vue – as if I wasn’t already there. The film was half an hour late to its own showing when it finally started at 7.45pm.</p><p>I am sick and tired of cinemas getting away with such treachery. I don’t want to follow in the footsteps of my friend, who knows that the ads at her local run for 22 minutes so slinks in at just the right time. I shouldn’t have to do mental maths because I am being lied to by cinemas.       <description><p>For more than three decades, Michael Gove has been a leading figure in British Conservatism. As a journalist, government minister and now editor of the Tory bible, the Spectator, he has helped shape the right even as it has moved further rightwards. In the latest episode of Radical Thinking, Gove joins Aditya Chakrabortty to discuss the future of the right, his record on Brexit and austerity, and the Spectator’s position on Islam</p><p>Watch the full episode with Michael Gove <a href="https://youtu.be/cIGXagkUFr8">here</a>.
 <br>
 <br>
 Aditya’s suggested reading:</p><p>To read the fruits of Michael Gove’s dalliance with the Marxism Today gang, look up his essay in a 1998 collection called The Moderniser’s Dilemma: Radical Politics in the Age of Blair</p><p>For slalom ride through Michael Gove’s years in power, read <a href="https://www.lrb.co.uk/the-paper/v41/n17/richard-j.-evans/the-demented-dalek">The Demented Dalek</a> by the historian Richard J Evans in the London Review of Books</p><p>To learn more on what’s become of the British right, there’s a <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfree/2024/sep/12/tory-leadership-jenrick-tugendhat-cleverly-badenoch">column by me </a>for the Guardian</p><p>Just why the most successful political party is now failing is analysed in-depth by Phil Burton-Cartledge in his book <a href="https://guardianbookshop.com/the-partys-over-9781839760372/">The Party’s Over: The Rise and Fall of the Conservatives from Thatcher to Sunak</a></p><p>Phil also writes a very good blog on British politics, which keeps a close eye on how each party is trying to marshall a coalition of voters. <a href="https://averypublicsociologist.blogspot.com/2026/10/the-clear-blue-water-strategy.html">Here</a> he is on Kemi Badenoch</p><p>Geoffrey Wheatcroft does an entertaining short narrative in <a href="https://guardianbookshop.com/bloody-panico-9781804295755/">Bloody Panico!:</a></p><p><a href="https://guardianbookshop.com/bloody-panico-9781804295755/">or, Whatever Happened to The Tory Party</a></p><p>For more on the economics of the Cameron years, <a href="https://foundationaleconomy.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/01/wp87.pdf">this paper</a> is acute on how the Tories failed to move the UK away from being a country of renters towards a country of makers. Two of its authors will join us for a podcast later in the series.</p><p>And if you want to read how Brexit may have cost the UK 8% of GDP, there’s <a href="https://www.nber.org/papers/w34459?st_source=ai_overview">this paper</a> based on data from the Bank of England</p><p>Finally, on the Spectator read Nesrine Malik’s recent column in The Guardian</p><p><a href="https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfree/2026/jul/20/islamophobia-spectator-britain-oldest-political-magazine">Why has Britain’s oldest political magazine become such a rabid cheerleader for Islamophobia?</a></p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/politics/commentisfree/audio/2026/oct/17/austerity-is-inevitably-painful-how-michael-gove-justifies-his-politics-radical-thinking-with-aditya-chakrabortty-podcast">Continue reading...</a></description>
